 NEW YORK (AP) — A rebound for several influential Big Tech stocks is helping to lift the U.S. market on Tuesday despite a fall for Apple and mixed trading elsewhere on Wall Street.
 The S&P 500 rose 0.5%, even though more stocks fell within the index than rose. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 247 points, or 0.5%, as of 12:21 p.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 1% higher.

 The stock market has been shaky recently as technology and artificial-intelligence stocks have swung on worries their prices shot too high in the frenzy around AI. Several of the most influential AI-related stocks held firmer Tuesday, which supported the market, after flipping from gains in the morning to losses in the afternoon a day earlier.
 Nvidia rose 3.2% and was the strongest force pushing upward on the S&P 500 Tuesday. Close behind were gains of 3.2% for Broadcom 5.5% for Advanced Micro Devices and 2.6% for Micron Technology.
 Apple was long seen on Wall Street as a Big Tech company that’s less dependent on AI. But it’s still feeling the effects of the AI boom.
 Memory chips for computers have become more expensive because of the demand created by the rush to build AI data centers. Those additional expenses are hitting Apple, which said it expects to make less profit from each $1 of its revenue during the final three months of this year.
 That helped send Apple’s stock down 2%, even though the seller of iPhones and Mac computers reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected.
 Palantir Technologies fell 2.1% even though it likewise reported a better profit than expected. The software company said it made more money working with U.S. companies than from the U.S. government for the first time, as U.S. commercial revenue soared 148% from a year earlier.
 Tuesday’s midterm elections may also be keeping financial markets unsteady, but history suggests they may not matter much for the broad market. Going back to 1970, the S&P 500 has had a positive return in the six months following a midterm election every time, according to Brock Weimer, an analyst at Edward Jones.
 Some on Wall Street speculate that a Democratic sweep of Congress this time around could lead to more regulations and restrictions on AI development. But Donald Trump would still be president and have the power to veto. And Wall Street generally prefers split control of Washington, which it sees as offering less risk of transformative policies that could reshape the economy.
 On the winning side of Wall Street Tuesday were stocks of several companies that reported stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected.
 Celanese climbed 4.7%, and DuPont added 8.8%.
 Revvity jumped 11.7% for one of the biggest gains in the S&P 500 after the life sciences company topped analysts’ expectations and CEO Prahlad Singh said end market conditions are continuing to improve.
 Expectations are high for all kinds of companies to continue to deliver big gains in profits as the U.S. economy keeps chugging along, even with high inflation and elevated interest rates. That helped send the S&P 500 to a record high last month.
 An encouraging report on the U.S. job market said Tuesday that employers were advertising more job openings at the end of September than economists expected. That helped push the yield on the 10-year Treasury up to 4.96% from 4.91% late Monday.
 In the oil market, prices continued to swing. Brent climbed above $107 per barrel overnight before briefly dropping below $101 in the morning amid continued uncertainty about what will happen in the war with Iran. It was most recently down 1.4% at $103.27.
 In stock markets abroad, indexes were lower across Europe and mixed in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.6% for one of the world’s sharpest moves following losses for its two tech giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.
 Stocks rose 0.3% in Australia after the country’s central bank raised its benchmark interest rate for the fifth time this year.
 AP Writers Elaine Lai, David McHugh and Rod McGuirk contributed to this report.

 Jury begins deliberating at Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault trial
 LONDON (AP) — Jurors began considering their verdicts on Tuesday in the trial of Russell Brand on charges of rape and sexual assault.
 After three weeks of argument and evidence, Judge Joel Bennathan told the jury at London’s Southwark Crown Court that they must reach a unanimous decision.
 “I can only accept a verdict that is the verdict of all 12 of you,” he said.
 After about an hour of deliberations, the jurors were sent home for the night with a warning not to discuss the case with anyone else.
 Brand, who is free on bail, has attended court every day, accompanied by his wife, Laura Gallacher.
 Six women, who don't know one another, accuse the actor-comedian of sexual misconduct between 1999 and 2009, a decade when Brand went from rising stand-up comedian to major celebrity in the U.K.
 Prosecutors argued that during that time Brand was “a sexual predator” who attacked the women in a hotel room, the London offices of MTV, the toilet of a London bar, a radio station, a recording studio and his home.
 Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault.
 Giving evidence, the entertainer acknowledged that he had been obsessed with sex as a younger man, but said his encounters were always consensual.
 Brand’s lawyers argued that the claimants’ cases were undermined by the fact that they only went to police years after the alleged assaults, and following the broadcast of a 2023 documentary that contained anonymous allegations against Brand.
 Brand’s lawyer, Ian Winter, said the “well of justice had been corrupted and contaminated” by the documentary.
 In his closing statement on Monday, Winter said the jury must separate Brand’s treatment of women from the question of whether he committed crimes.
 “It is not criminal to treat women unkindly before, during or after sex,” he said. “It is not, I am afraid, criminal to be disrespectful or rude or to act like a crazy idiot.”
 He said Brand “had an immense amount of sex and none of it was unlawful.”
 “Disgusting, distasteful, immoral, who cares?” the lawyer said. “It’s irrelevant to your consideration.”
 Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek” and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.
 In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.
